question: Poland needs to bring its legislation in line with the Digital Services Act (DSA). As part of the process, it is amending its Electronic Services Act.

The draft revision of this act prepared by the Ministry of Digital Affairs, as the ministry responsible, envisages empowering the President of the Office of Electronic Communications to issue orders expressly blocking online content in the context of administrative proceedings.

Concerns have been raised, including by experts, about the possible misuse of this measure to restrict freedom of speech online and censure (albeit lawful) content and material criticising, for example, government policy, politicians or other public figures. 1.

Does the Commission believe that such a legal solution could be deemed a threat to the legal guarantee of freedom of speech, particularly as the President of the Office of Electronic Communications is appointed and dismissed by the Sejm on the motion of the Prime Minister, laying their decisions open to political pressure.

In the Commission’s view, is the mechanism put forward by the Ministry of Digital Affairs for removing online content compatible with the objectives and scope of the DSA, and also with the guarantee of the freedom of expression, particularly as any appeal against a decision of the President of the Office of Electronic Communications will be subject to only a secondary limited judicial review, and the procedure determining the illegality of content will take place without the involvement of the author of the content at issue?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.3.2025) The Commission acknowledges Poland’s efforts to align its legislation with the Digital Services Act (DSA)1.

Commission takes note of the information available to it regarding the proposed amendments to the Electronic Services Act to establish an administrative procedure allowing the President of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) to issue removal orders against certain types of illegal content aiming to ensure a swift and predictable response to uphold legal standards.

At this stage of draft legislation, the Commission has not performed a formal assessment of their compatibility with EU law which would take place in the context of the notification requirements set out in the Single Market Transparency Directive2. The DSA does not empower national authorities to issue orders against illegal content but acknowledges that they may do so based on other applicable national or EU laws.

When such orders fulfil the conditions set out in Article 9 of the DSA, this Regulation sets out an obligation for the providers concerned to inform the issuing authority of any effect given to those orders. The absence of content authors’ involvement prevents delays but must be complemented by fair appeal mechanisms allowing the affected provider and users to seek redress.

The DSA sets out clear independence criteria that the President of the Office of Electronic Communications as Digital Services Coordinator under the DSA needs to abide by. The Commission will remain vigilant concerning compliance with the transparency requirements for Digital Services Coordinators under the DSA.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1–102: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng 2 Directive (EU) 2015/1535 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 September 2015 laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical regulations and of rules on Information Society services OJ L 241, 17.9.2015, p. 1–15: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2015/1535/oj/eng
